entries.title: Hebrew at a glance
body: Modern Hebrew is a Semitic language, related to Arabic and Aramaic, and the main language of Israel. It was revived as an everyday spoken language in the late 19th and early 20th centuries after centuries of use mainly in prayer and writing.

Words are built from roots of three consonants: כ־ת־ב (k-t-v) gives כותב “writes”, מכתב “letter” and כתובת “address”. Nouns, adjectives and verbs mark masculine or feminine, and the present tense has no verb “to be”.

entries.title: The alef-bet
body: Hebrew has 22 letters, all consonants, written right to left. There are no capitals. Five letters take a different shape at the end of a word: כ ך, מ ם, נ ן, פ ף, צ ץ.
A few letters also stand for vowels: ו for o or u, י for i or e. The letters ב, כ and פ have two sounds each (b/v, k/ch, p/f).

entries.title: Vowel points
entries.body: Vowels can be shown with dots and dashes under, over or inside the letters (ניקוד, niqqud). Children's books, poetry, prayer books and dictionaries use them; newspapers, signs and everyday writing leave them out, and readers fill in the vowels from context.

examples.e: the same word with and without vowel points
book · barber · frontier: all written ספר without points

entries.title: Sounds to watch
entries.body: Modern Israeli Hebrew has five vowels: a, e, i, o, u. The stress usually falls on the last syllable. Two pairs of letters now sound the same for most speakers: ח and כ (ch), and א and ע (silent or a light catch). ר is said in the throat, like French r.

examples.e: hot · how much (ח and כ both ch / k)

entries.title: Personal pronouns
entries.body: “You” and “they” have separate masculine and feminine forms. A mixed group takes the masculine.

entries.title: The present tense
entries.body: The present tense has four forms, chosen by the gender and number of the subject, not by the person. Past and future, which come later, change for person too.

entries.title: את before a definite object
entries.body: When the object of a verb is definite (it has ה־, or it is a name), Hebrew puts the little word את (et) in front of it. With an indefinite object there is no את. It has no English translation.

entries.title: Numbers
entries.body: Numbers have masculine and feminine forms. Counting aloud, telling the time and saying prices use the feminine forms shown here.

examples.e: Excuse me, where is the station?
Have a peaceful Sabbath! (Friday and Saturday)

entries.title: The Israeli week
entries.body: The working week runs Sunday to Thursday, and Friday is a short day. Shabbat runs from sunset on Friday to nightfall on Saturday; many shops and most public transport stop. The days are numbered: יום ראשון “first day” is Sunday, יום שני Monday, and so on to יום שישי, Friday.
